the way ....name: "how" in place of "the way"
the way ....how: CT, 27 Nov: The way can change to "how". As in "how it usually did". Swap the two words and soften the absolute if there is one.
the way ....before: Then she smiled, and the whole kitchen came up a notch, the way it always had.
the way ....after: Then she smiled, and the whole kitchen came up a notch, how it usually did.

the way ....name: "same as"
the way ....how: For a habit somebody has always had. Plain, spoken.
the way ....before: ate her ice cream out of the little tub, the way she had every night of his life.
the way ....after: ate her ice cream out of the little tub, same as every night of his life.

the way ....name: "like"
the way ....how: The plain spoken comparison. Check the paragraph does not already have a "like" simile. Capped low: CT passed over "like it always did" for his own "how it usually did" (27 Nov).

the way ....name: The storyteller turns to the reader
the way ....how: Break the comparison off into a short sentence of its own, said to the reader. CT's own lines do this: "You don't see those anymore."
the way ....before: Elijah found out the rest in pieces, the way you do in a cab.
the way ....after: Elijah found out the rest in pieces. Cabs are good for that.

the way ....name: The verb carries the comparison
the way ....how: Find the one verb that does what the comparison was explaining, and let the thing itself act. Not a cleverer line: a plainer one with a verb that moves. (The earlier example, "checked him for ripeness", was a clever line and came out, 27 Nov.)
the way ....before: (CT's own example of the move, from his note on smell) The perfume ...
the way ....after: "acts like a lightning rod for knuckleheads and more or less behaves like a slime mold, expanding out in every direction, but ... is utterly decimated by the ferocity of the air from the kitchen."

the way ....name: Cut the tail
the way ....how: When the image before the comma has already landed, stop the sentence there.
the way ....before: the whole kitchen came up a notch, the way it always had.
the way ....after: the whole kitchen came up a notch.

looked at him/her/it.name: Let the next line imply the look
looked at him/her/it.how: If the line of talk after it only makes sense because somebody looked, cut the look.
looked at him/her/it.before: "Let's do a show together." / Elijah looked at him. / "I'm serious."

looked at him/her/it.name: The face does the work
looked at him/her/it.how: Say what the looker's face did, not that they looked.
looked at him/her/it.before: Trent looked at him like he'd answered in Portuguese.
looked at him/her/it.after: Trent's face went blank, like he'd answered in Portuguese.

looked at him/her/it.name: Say what the eyes land on
looked at him/her/it.how: Name the one thing seen, or what the person does with it, so the look turns into finding something out.
looked at him/her/it.before: Elijah looked at the thermos for a while.
looked at him/her/it.after: Elijah read what was left of the name.
looked at him/her/it.note: The example line itself stays in the book (Claude, 27 Nov: the pause before "Wait" is the joke; Gus not pressing is the point). It shows the move only.

looked at him/her/it.name: The thing pulls the eye
looked at him/her/it.how: Make the thing looked at the subject. It draws, catches or holds the eye.
looked at him/her/it.before: Elijah looked at the thermos for a while.
looked at him/her/it.after: The thermos kept catching Elijah's eye.
looked at him/her/it.note: The example line itself stays in the book (Claude, 27 Nov: the pause before "Wait" is the joke; Gus not pressing is the point). It shows the move only.

for a while / a long time.name: Measure the time with a thing
for a while / a long time.how: Use what goes by: miles, orchards, a song, a cup going cold. Take it from the place and the hour.
for a while / a long time.before: They rode a while. There were almond orchards on both sides, in rows so straight they flickered.
for a while / a long time.after: They rode through a few miles of almonds, in rows so straight they flickered.

for a while / a long time.name: Say what he keeps doing
for a while / a long time.how: "Kept" plus the action holds the time without counting it.
for a while / a long time.before: Elijah looked at the thermos for a while.
for a while / a long time.after: Elijah kept looking at the thermos.
for a while / a long time.note: The example line itself stays in the book (Claude, 27 Nov: the pause before "Wait" is the joke; Gus not pressing is the point). It shows the move only.

for a while / a long time.name: Cut it
for a while / a long time.how: When the next sentence already makes the pause (a new paragraph, a line of talk that comes late), drop the measure.

didn't say anything.name: Say what they did instead
didn't say anything.how: The silence is a choice. Show the small thing done in place of talking.
didn't say anything.before: Elijah wrote the question down. Gus glanced over and didn't say anything.
didn't say anything.after: Elijah wrote the question down. Gus glanced over and let him write.
didn't say anything.note: The example line itself stays in the book (Claude, 27 Nov: the pause before "Wait" is the joke; Gus not pressing is the point). It shows the move only.

didn't say anything.name: Send the eyes somewhere
didn't say anything.how: They look back at the work, the road, the plate.
didn't say anything.before: Gus glanced over and didn't say anything.
didn't say anything.after: Gus glanced over and went back to the road.
didn't say anything.note: The example line itself stays in the book (Claude, 27 Nov: the pause before "Wait" is the joke; Gus not pressing is the point). It shows the move only.

didn't say anything.name: A verb that makes it a choice
didn't say anything.how: An idiom from the person's own trade for letting a thing go.
didn't say anything.before: Gus glanced over and didn't say anything.
didn't say anything.after: Gus glanced over and let it ride.
didn't say anything.note: The example line itself stays in the book (Claude, 27 Nov: the pause before "Wait" is the joke; Gus not pressing is the point). It shows the move only.

didn't say anything.name: Give the silence to the room
didn't say anything.how: Name the sound that is left when nobody talks, the one that belongs to that place and hour. The book already leans on things that tick; pick another.

He knew / didn't know.name: Put it in his own head-voice
He knew / didn't know.how: Say the thought the way he would think it, with no "He knew" in front.
He knew / didn't know.before: Elijah didn't know what one of those was worth. He knew it was more than he had.
He knew / didn't know.after: Whatever one of those was worth, it was more than he had.

He knew / didn't know.name: Fold two sentences into one
He knew / didn't know.how: For a didn't-know then knew pair: one sentence, joined with "only that" or "but".
He knew / didn't know.before: Elijah didn't know what one of those was worth. He knew it was more than he had.
He knew / didn't know.after: Elijah didn't know what one of those was worth, only that it was more than he had.

He knew / didn't know.name: State the fact flat
He knew / didn't know.how: Drop "He knew" and say the thing. The book sits on his shoulder, so a flat fact is already his.

He knew / didn't know.name: "he thought" or "he figured"
He knew / didn't know.how: The guide: "He thought" and "he felt" are CT's and are allowed. Use them when it is a guess, not a fact.

Then he/she.name: Join it with "and"
Then he/she.how: Two steps by one person become one sentence.

Then he/she.name: Cut "Then"
Then he/she.how: When the order is already plain, start with the person or the thing.

Then he/she.name: Start with the thing
Then he/she.how: Open on what the sentence is about: the object, the place, the line of talk (guide, section 10).

not X. It's Y.name: Say only the Y
not X. It's Y.how: The guide keeps the mirrored contrast out of Claude's wording. Drop the X and say what the thing is.
not X. It's Y.before: It wasn't a salary. It was an insurance policy, something to stand on if the floor went out.
not X. It's Y.after: The two spares would be his insurance policy, something to stand on if the floor went out.

not X. It's Y.name: Give the X to a person
not X. It's Y.how: If the X is worth keeping, let somebody say it or assume it out loud, and let the narration give the Y.

not X. It's Y.name: One sentence with "more ... than"
not X. It's Y.how: "It was more an insurance policy than a salary." One sentence, no bounce.

nodded / shrugged.name: Let them say it
nodded / shrugged.how: A nod is a yes and a shrug is a don't-know. Give the word or two the person would say.

nodded / shrugged.name: Another part of the body
nodded / shrugged.how: CT: "Simple physical actions that make sense and add character." A hand, a chin, a boot, the thing they are holding. Check the next few lines do not already have the same beat.

nodded / shrugged.name: Cut it
nodded / shrugged.how: When the line of talk already answers, the nod is extra.

nodded / shrugged.name: Keep the nod, add what it is like
nodded / shrugged.how: The book's own good one: "Gus nodded like they were neighbors." Only when the comparison tells you something about the person.
